title: Turner Syndrome Lost to Follow-Up / Chest Pain and an Overdue Aortic Scan

blocks.text: Turner Syndrome Lost to Follow-Up / Chest Pain and an Overdue Aortic Scan

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-21 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: International Turner syndrome guideline: Gravholt CH et al., Eur J Endocrinol 2024;190(6):G53-G151; AHA scientific statement, Cardiovascular health in Turner syndrome (Silberbach et al., 2018); ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases (2024) · Related AMaC: AMaC premature ovarian insufficiency and coarctation stations; this one tests adult Turner syndrome follow-up

Dear Doctor, a 28-year-old accountant. Turner syndrome was diagnosed at 14. She was lost to follow-up after leaving paediatric care and stopped her oestrogen two years ago. Blood pressure at her GP was 152/90. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A woman with Turner syndrome who has been lost to follow-up needs a catch-up of heart, aorta, blood pressure, bones and hormones. Any chest pain in Turner syndrome is a possible aortic problem and needs same-day assessment.

The Examiner Trap. She mentions a sudden chest pain two days ago only when asked. Candidates tidy up the hormone and screening plan and forget the aorta. Pass: chest pain asked, same-day emergency assessment with aortic imaging, blood pressure, oestrogen. Fail: routine clinic only.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Ask about chest pain, breathlessness, her periods and oestrogen, then the screening she has missed.
"Have you had any chest pain or breathlessness? When did you stop oestrogen? Any hearing, thyroid, bowel or sugar problems?"
Chest pain; breathlessness; oestrogen; periods; bones; hearing; coeliac; thyroid; glucose; mood.
Check the build, the neck, the blood pressure and the heart, and look for other features of the syndrome.
"May I check your height, neck, blood pressure and heart? Tell me if anything hurts."
Height; neck; hairline; chest; elbows; blood pressure both arms; heart; pulses; cover her.
Explain what the syndrome needs in adults, why the aorta is the priority and what happens next.
"That pain may be your aorta, so I want a scan today, blood pressure control and a plan to restart oestrogen."
Same-day emergency assessment; aortic imaging; blood pressure; then oestrogen, thyroid, glucose, coeliac, bones, hearing, review.

D
Differential diagnosis
Calls the chest pain anxiety or muscular.
Sudden chest pain through to the back in Turner syndrome could be aortic dissection or another aortic problem, which imaging must exclude.
Also names coarctation, a bicuspid valve and ischaemia, and links raised blood pressure to the kidneys and the aorta.

Asks for a chest X-ray only.
Asks for same-day aortic imaging (CT aortography, or as the emergency team advises), ECG, troponin, and blood tests: thyroid function, HbA1c, glucose, liver enzymes and transglutaminase antibody.
Also asks for a DEXA scan and an audiology review.

Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): sends her away as routine after a sudden chest pain, with no same-day aortic imaging.
Arranges same-day emergency assessment with aortic imaging, blood pressure control, and says to call 999 for chest pain, back pain or breathlessness.
Also says the aorta is monitored every 5 to 10 years once the baseline is normal, and restarts oestrogen under specialist care.

Asks what worries her, acknowledges both and explains that regular care reduces the risk.

Explains the scan, the blood pressure plan and the hormone plan, and asks her view.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 28-year-old accountant. You are quiet, a little guarded and have avoided hospitals since leaving paediatrics.
Opening line: "My GP made me come about my blood pressure. I haven't been seen by anyone for Turner's for years."
Volunteered: you stopped your oestrogen two years ago because you felt fine and did not want to be reminded.
Only if asked: two days ago you had a sudden sharp pain in your chest that went through to your back. It settled after about ten minutes. You felt faint.
Only if asked about other symptoms: tired. You have not had your thyroid or sugar checked. Your hearing is slightly worse. No coeliac symptoms.

Background, only if asked: no regular medicines since stopping oestrogen. No allergies. Never smoked. A glass of wine at weekends. No recent travel. No family history of heart disease. You live alone in a flat.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of dying young and of never having children. Say: "I read that women with Turner's can die suddenly."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is the chest pain serious?" "Do I have to go back on the hormones?" "Could I ever have a baby?"
How you react: if rushed, you retreat. If listened to and given a clear plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: short stature; webbed neck; low hairline; wide chest; respiratory rate 15; pulse 82 regular; blood pressure 152/90; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Femoral pulses present. Soft ejection systolic murmur. Chest clear.

Results, only when requested (recent GP results and clinic tests): ECG normal. GP bloods last month: TSH raised; HbA1c in the diabetic range (to be repeated to confirm); liver enzymes mildly raised; transglutaminase antibody negative. Aortic imaging is arranged the same day through the emergency team, so no scan result is available in the room.

Question ladder: 1. What could the chest pain be? (D, R4) Aortic dissection or another acute aortic problem; also coarctation, bicuspid valve, ischaemia. 2. Which scan and how soon? (E, R5) Same-day CT aortography through the emergency team, with ECG and troponin. 3. Which blood tests are due regularly? (E, R5) Thyroid function, HbA1c, liver enzymes, transglutaminase antibody. 4. How often is the aorta monitored? (E, R6) Every 5 to 10 years once the baseline is normal, sooner with risk factors. 5. What should she do if the pain returns? (E, R6) Call 999.

Curveballs: She asks to postpone the scan until after her holiday: no, her pain needs imaging today. She asks about pregnancy: spontaneous pregnancy is uncommon and pregnancy carries a high aortic risk, so she needs specialist reproductive and cardio-obstetric counselling, with aortic imaging first. She becomes breathless in clinic: emergency care.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about chest pain, breathlessness and stopping oestrogen (C)
Checks blood pressure and examines the heart and pulses (A)
Finds short stature, webbed neck and raised blood pressure (B)
Considers aortic dissection for chest pain in Turner syndrome (D)
Requests same-day aortic imaging through the emergency team (E)
Arranges thyroid, glucose, liver, coeliac, bone and hearing checks (E)
Says seek immediate care for chest pain or breathlessness (E)
Restarts oestrogen under specialist care (E)
Asks what worries her and offers a fertility discussion (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lift your top. [R1 Fail] Are your periods regular? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the heart.) [R3 Fail] The chest pain is anxiety. [R4 Fail] A chest X-ray. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Restart oestrogen and come back next year. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] See your GP. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): sudden chest pain through to the back in Turner syndrome needs same-day aortic imaging. No consent, the heart skipped, and the aorta missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your blood pressure and heart? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Any chest pain or breathlessness? When did you stop oestrogen? Any thyroid, sugar or hearing problems? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Two days ago a sudden pain went through to my back. I stopped oestrogen two years ago.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, then covers her and thanks her.) A webbed neck, short stature, raised blood pressure and a soft murmur. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Chest pain like that could be an aortic problem, so I need to rule out dissection. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A scan of the aorta today, an ECG and troponin, and blood tests for thyroid, sugar, liver and coeliac. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I'd send you to the emergency department today for a scan of your aorta, get your blood pressure controlled, and ask you to call 999 if the pain or breathlessness returns. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: Dying young, and never having children.
CANDIDATE: Both are fair; regular care lowers the risk. [R7 Pass] Are you happy to go to the emergency department today while we arrange the rest? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Treated the chest pain as urgent and planned the scan and tests. Did not name the surveillance interval, bones or hearing.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll ask about periods and fertility only with your permission. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any fractures or low mood? What are your wishes about a family? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Blood pressure in both arms and the femoral pulses. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Dissection, coarctation, a bicuspid valve and ischaemia; raised blood pressure adds to the aortic risk. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: A DEXA scan and an audiology review as well. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Once the baseline is normal we'll monitor the aorta every five to ten years, and restart oestrogen under the specialist. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: We can arrange a specialist fertility discussion. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and an annual review. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, fractures and mood, both-arm blood pressure, other causes, bones and hearing, surveillance interval and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about chest pain. In Turner syndrome it may be the aorta.
R4: Calling it anxiety. Sudden chest pain through to the back needs aortic imaging.
R5: Asking only for a chest X-ray. CT or MR angiography is needed to show the aorta.
R6: Treating the visit as routine. Same-day imaging and clear return advice are needed.
"Can I ask whether you've had any chest pain?"
"That pain could be the aorta, so I'd like to scan it."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

International Turner syndrome guideline (Gravholt 2024): lifelong heart surveillance; cardiac MRI (or ECG-gated CT if MRI is not tolerated) for adolescents and adults newly diagnosed, echocardiography at least every 5 to 10 years in adults, and lifelong surveillance at a frequency set by dissection risk factors (recommendations 4.8, 4.10, 4.11 and 4.13); an aortic size index above 2.0 cm/m2 is dilatation. New chest or back pain, or breathlessness, may be aortic dissection and needs emergency assessment; CT aortography is the usual first imaging for a suspected acute aortic syndrome (ESC 2024).

Regular checks (Gravholt 2024 and local protocol): thyroid function, HbA1c, liver enzymes, coeliac serology, blood pressure, hearing and bone health. Oestrogen replacement is central to bone and general health and should be restarted and continued under specialist care.

AHA scientific statement (Silberbach 2018): index aortic size to body surface area; uncontrolled hypertension raises the risk of aortic enlargement and dissection; a young woman with chest pain may not be assessed for dissection unless the clinician thinks of it.
THINK: Turner, chest pain: an aortic problem to exclude today.
SAY: "I'd like a scan of your aorta today."
DO: Ask about chest pain; blood pressure in both arms.
NUMBERS: Aorta imaging every 5 to 10 years once the baseline is normal (Gravholt 2024).
TRAP: Routine clinic; no aorta.
FINISH: Same-day aortic imaging, blood pressure, regular bloods, oestrogen.

Gravholt CH et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the care of girls and women with Turner syndrome. Eur J Endocrinol 2024;190(6):G53-G151. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11759048/ Supports: Surveillance of the aorta, risk factors for dissection, blood pressure, oestrogen and regular screening.

Silberbach M et al. Cardiovascular health in Turner syndrome: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Circ Genom Precis Med 2018;11:e000048. https://doi.org/10.1161/HCG.0000000000000048 Supports: Aortic size index, hypertension and dissection risk, and recognising chest pain.

Mazzolai L et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases. Eur Heart J 2024;45(36):3538-3700. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae179 Supports: CT aortography as first-line imaging for suspected acute aortic syndrome (full text not readable; confirmed from a secondary commentary, ECR Journal, 29 November 2024).
